property_summary: For every initial state the reference contract's owner() returns the stored _owner value (including when _owner is address(0) it returns address(0) as _owner), whereas the mutant changes owner() behavior so it may return address(0) only when _owner is zero — the distinguishing rule is that calling owner() always returns the actual stored owner value; the mutant still returns same for nonzero but the test will detect that after transferOwnership(address(0)) the reference still returns address(0) (stored) while mutant may differ (we assert owner() equals c.owner() stored behavior via performing a transfer to zero and checking owner()), i.e., the test asserts owner() equals the stored owner observable after transferOwnership to arbitrary address, and the mutant breaks for some fuzzed inputs.

For any address x set via transferOwnership(x), calling owner() must return that exact stored owner value; the mutant returns address(0) whenever the stored owner is zero but otherwise may differ, so there exists an x (namely address(0)) where the mutant's owner() output diverges from the stored owner.

For every address newOwner provided, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the public owner() getter must return exactly the stored owner value (i.e. the same address passed); the mutant incorrectly collapses some stored owners to address(0) causing owner() to return address(0) when the stored owner was set to address(0) (or otherwise diverge).

For every address provided to transferOwnership(newOwner), calling owner() immediately after must return exactly that same address; the mutant collapses some stored owners to address(0) causing owner() to return address(0) instead of the stored value for at least some inputs.

For any address newOwner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the public owner() getter must return exactly the stored owner value (i.e. the same address set); the mutant changes owner() so it may return address(0) even when the stored owner is non-zero, causing a mismatch for some fuzzed inputs.

For every caller and execution context, the correct contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (_owner) while the mutant that returns tx.origin will, for some callers (e.g., when called via an intermediate contract), return a different address; the test checks that owner() equals the deployer (owner) when called directly and thus will fail for a mutant that returns tx.origin when invoked via a contract call.

For any caller address X, when the saved owner getter is invoked via a direct call from X (i.e., tx.origin == X and msg.sender == X) and also via an intermediate contract that forwards the call (so msg.sender is the forwarder but tx.origin == original caller), the correct contract always returns the same owner value (the stored _owner) for both direct and forwarded calls; the mutant that returns tx.origin will return different values when the call is forwarded (it will return the original EOA instead of the stored owner), so there exists some caller and forwarder setup that makes the mutant disagree while the reference always returns the stored owner.

For every caller (EOA or contract) invoking owner(), the genuine contract always returns the stored owner address (_owner) whereas the mutant that returns tx.origin will return a different value when called through an intermediate contract (tx.origin != _owner) — so there exists a forwarded call scenario where the mutant's return differs while the reference always returns the stored owner.

For every caller address A, calling c.owner() directly or via any intermediary contract must always return the same stored owner value (the owner set at initialization); the mutant that returns tx.origin can be made to return a different value when called through a forwarding contract (tx.origin != stored owner), violating this invariance.

For every caller address, the reference contract's owner() always returns the stored owner address (the deployer) regardless of whether the call is direct or proxied; the mutant that returns tx.origin can be made to return a different address when called through a proxy contract, so there exists a proxied call where owner() differs.

For any caller, the reference contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (_owner) (independent of msg.sender), whereas the mutant incorrectly returns msg.sender, so there exists a caller address for which owner() differs between reference and mutant.

For any caller address, the reference contract returns a fixed stored owner address (the deployer) from owner(), whereas the mutant incorrectly returns msg.sender, so there exists some caller for which owner() differs (i.e. caller != stored owner).

For every caller, the reference contract's owner() returns the same fixed owner address (the stored _owner) regardless of msg.sender; the mutant returns msg.sender instead and thus for some caller addresses owner() differs from the stored owner.

For any newOwner address, the reference contract rejects setting owner to the zero address (transferOwnership(address(0)) reverts) while the mutant allows transferring ownership to the zero address (succeeds), so the reference always prevents owner becoming address(0) but the mutant can make owner == address(0) for some input.

For any caller who is the current owner and any non-zero newOwner address, calling transferOwnership always updates owner() to newOwner (and thus ownership changes even if newOwner equals current owner), while the mutant prevents the state change when newOwner equals current owner; therefore there exist inputs (newOwner == current owner) where mutant's owner() remains unchanged although reference still sets/transitions owner to same value and emits OwnershipTransferred.

For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner ≠ address(0), calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference always performs the state-changing _transferOwnership (and thus sets owner() to newOwner and emits OwnershipTransferred); the mutant skips _transferOwnership when newOwner == current owner, so for that input the mutant's observable owner() change/transfer behavior differs (the reference still executes the transfer flow even when newOwner equals current owner).

For any caller that is the current owner and any newOwner address (non-zero) the reference contract always performs the ownership transfer operation (i.e. calls _transferOwnership) so that an OwnershipTransferred event is emitted and owner() remains equal to the caller after transferOwnership(owner) (the observable owner() remains set and event semantics occur); the mutant skips calling _transferOwnership when newOwner == _owner, so invoking transferOwnership with newOwner equal to the current owner yields a different observable behavior (mutant does not perform the transfer action while the reference still does).

For any nonzero newOwner and when called by the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract always executes the state-changing _transferOwnership path (observable via an emitted OwnershipTransferred event and by reading owner()) while the mutant skips performing _transferOwnership when newOwner equals the current owner; thus there exists an input (newOwner == current owner) where the mutant's observable behavior differs (it does not emit/perform the transfer) even though the reference always executes the transfer path.

For any non-zero newOwner and when called by the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always results in owner() being equal to newOwner afterwards in the reference; the mutant skips the internal transfer when newOwner equals the current owner, so there exist inputs (newOwner == current owner) where the mutant's observable owner() does not reflect that the transfer path was executed (i.e. it does not perform the transfer action), violating the rule.

Invariant: transferOwnership when called by the current owner (msg.sender == owner) always succeeds; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead can cause transferOwnership to fail when a contract (not EOA) calls transferOwnership even if that contract was invoked by the owner, so some inputs (contract caller addresses) make the mutant reject a valid owner-invoked transfer.

For any caller address X (possibly a contract) and any newOwner Y, if X is the current owner then calling transferOwnership(Y) through X should succeed on the reference contract; the mutant that compares tx.origin instead of msg.sender will cause such a call to fail when X is a contract (even if tx.origin == owner), so there exist inputs (contract caller addresses) where the mutant reverts while the reference succeeds.

For any caller address X and newOwner Y, if X is the current owner then calling transferOwnership(Y) through X should succeed on the reference implementation; the mutant that uses tx.origin instead of msg.sender may cause such a call to revert when X is a contract (even if the EOA tx.origin == owner), so there exist contract caller inputs where the mutant fails while the reference succeeds.

Any caller who is the current owner (msg.sender == owner) can successfully call transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference contract; the mutant that additionally requires tx.origin == owner will fail when the owner is a contract calling through an EOA origin, so transferOwnership may revert for some contract callers.

For any caller address X that is equal to owner(), calling transferOwnership(newOwner) through X always succeeds on the reference contract (permission is based on msg.sender == owner); the mutant that additionally checks tx.origin can fail when the call is made by a contract (msg.sender == owner but tx.origin != owner), so some contract-call inputs make transferOwnership revert on the mutant while the reference succeeds.

For every input the reference contract returns the actual paused state (paused() == vaultPaused), but the mutant always returns true; therefore there exists inputs where paused() differs (e.g., after unpause the reference returns false while mutant returns true).

For any initial keeper address and any boolean unpauseDecision, calling pause()/unpause() via the keeper causes C.paused() to reflect the actual paused state (i.e., paused() == expectedPaused after operations); the mutant that forces paused() to always return true violates this when expectedPaused is false (after unpause).

For any nonzero newKeeper address passed to setKeeper by the owner, the contract's keeper becomes that address; the mutant rejects zero address inputs and thus for some inputs (owner calling with address(0)) the mutant's keeper remains unchanged while the reference sets keeper to address(0).
For any caller who is the owner, calling setKeeper(x) always sets keeper() == x in the reference; the mutant rejects x == address(0) and thus for owner-calls with x == address(0) keeper differs.

For every caller who is the contract owner, calling setKeeper(newKeeper) results in keeper() equaling newKeeper; the mutant rejects address(0) and thus for owner calling setKeeper(address(0)) the mutant leaves keeper unchanged while the reference sets it to address(0).

For any caller who is the contract owner, after calling setKeeper(newKeeper) the public keeper() getter equals newKeeper; the mutant changes this by reverting on or refusing to set address(0), so an owner call with newKeeper == address(0) will make the mutant leave keeper() unchanged while the reference sets it to address(0).

For any owner caller and any candidate keeper address k, calling setKeeper(k) always makes c.keeper() equal k in the reference implementation; the mutant instead forbids setting keeper to address(0) and thus for some k (k == address(0)) c.keeper() differs between reference and mutant.

For any caller that is the contract owner, calling setKeeper(x) sets keeper to the owner (the caller); the mutant erroneously sets keeper to msg.sender regardless of the provided _keeper argument, so when owner != _keeper the mutant's resulting keeper differs from the provided _keeper while the reference always sets keeper equal to the provided _keeper.

For any caller who is the contract owner and any address _keeper, the reference sets keeper == _keeper after setKeeper(_keeper) (mutant sets keeper == msg.sender, breaking this when msg.sender != _keeper).

For any caller that is the contract owner and any address _keeper, calling setKeeper(_keeper) causes the contract's keeper getter to equal the provided _keeper in the reference; the mutant instead sets keeper to msg.sender, violating this rule when msg.sender != _keeper.

For any caller who is the owner and any address _keeper, calling setKeeper(_keeper) results in c.keeper() == _keeper in the correct contract; the mutant instead sets keeper to msg.sender so when msg.sender != _keeper the mutant violates this property.

For any owner caller and any target address _keeper, calling setKeeper(_keeper) results in c.keeper() equaling the provided _keeper in the correct contract; the mutant instead sets keeper to msg.sender, so when msg.sender != _keeper the mutant violates this rule.

For any caller who is the owner, calling setKeeper(newKeeper) always updates the contract's keeper state to newKeeper (reference obeys this); the mutant emits the event but does not update keeper, violating this property for some inputs.

For any caller who is the contract owner and any address newKeeper, calling setKeeper(newKeeper) updates the public keeper state to newKeeper (reference C) but the mutant emits the event without updating state, so keeper differs for some inputs.

For any address newKeeper set by the contract owner via setKeeper(newKeeper), the reference updates the public keeper state to newKeeper; the mutant emits the event but fails to update keeper, so after the call keeper() != newKeeper for some inputs.

For any address newKeeper set by the contract owner via setKeeper(newKeeper), the reference updates the public keeper state to newKeeper; the mutant emits the event but fails to update keeper, so after the call keeper() == newKeeper in the reference but may differ in the mutant.

For any owner caller and any address newKeeper, calling setKeeper(newKeeper) updates the public keeper() to newKeeper in the correct contract; the mutant emits the event but does not change keeper(), so keeper() may remain unchanged for some inputs.

For any caller address x and newKeeper address k, only the contract owner (the deployer) can successfully change keeper via setKeeper in the correct contract; the mutant that removes the onlyOwner check allows non-owners to change keeper, so there exist caller/newKeeper pairs where keeper after the call differs between reference and mutant.

For every uint256 input x passed to setThresholds(x), the contract's public getter slippageThresholdGmxBps equals the exact input x (reference preserves value); the mutant that halves the assigned value will cause slippageThresholdGmxBps != x for some x (in fact for any x where x/2 != x).

For any provided threshold t, calling setThresholds(t) on the correct contract stores exactly t in slippageThresholdGmxBps; the mutant that assigns half the provided value will cause the stored value to differ from t for at least some t (e.g., any odd or nonzero t where t/2 != t).
